title: FDIC Proposes Weekly and Quarterly Reporting Forms for Stablecoin Issuers Under the GENIUS Act, Including Reserve-Asset Schedules, With Comments Due September 18
summary: The FDIC announced on July 17, 2026 proposed weekly (PS-01, PS-01a) and quarterly (PS-02) reporting forms for FDIC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act, covering reserve assets, issuance and redemptions, with comments due September 18 and an estimated burden of 3,840 hours a year across about 30 institutions.
description:
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation has published proposed reporting forms and instructions for stablecoin issuers that it supervises, as part of the U.S. implementation of the GENIUS Act, the law that set up a federal framework for payment stablecoins. According to a law-firm analysis by Orrick, the FDIC announced the notice on July 17, 2026, and the analysis was published on July 24. A summary from the Independent Community Bankers of America, dated July 20, 2026, reports the same action through a Financial Institution Letter. This article uses those two sources and notes that the exact date of the FDIC's issuance differs slightly between them, so it describes the notice as issued in mid-July 2026. The sources describe the forms at a high level and do not list every data field.

How the forms fit into the rulemaking

The reporting forms implement the FDIC's proposed rule of April 10, 2026, which set up the framework for permitted payment stablecoin issuers, abbreviated PPSIs. The ICBA summary says comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register, and the Orrick analysis gives the date as September 18. The sources describe the forms as proposed and not final.

According to Orrick, the stated purposes of the reports are to help the FDIC supervise issuers, promote transparency and check compliance with the reserve asset requirements. The reports would be confidential, yet the FDIC also plans to publish the quarterly data. The sources do not explain how those two statements fit together, so this article reports both as stated.

The weekly report

Each PPSI would file a separate weekly form for every payment stablecoin brand it issues. There are two versions. Form PS-01 is the full version. It applies to PPSIs with at least $1 billion in total outstanding issuance value, or at least $100 million in average daily transaction volume in the prior month. It has eight schedules that cover the largest holders and exchanges for a stablecoin, issuance and redemption activity, and reserve assets. The reserve schedules cover cash balances, U.S. Treasury securities, reverse repurchase agreements and money market mutual funds.

Form PS-01a is an abridged version for issuers below those thresholds, with three schedules. The FDIC may still require a smaller issuer to file the full form if supervisory needs call for it.

The two thresholds are alternatives, not cumulative: an issuer that crosses either the $1 billion issuance level or the $100 million daily volume level files the full form. A stablecoin with modest outstanding value but heavy trading could therefore still be subject to the more detailed weekly schedules. That is a reading of the thresholds as the sources state them, and the sources do not give an example.

The quarterly report

Form PS-02 would apply to all PPSIs. It is a streamlined version of the call report that banks file, with five schedules: the income statement, the balance sheet, off-balance-sheet items, capital and operational backstop, and additional memorandum data. The FDIC plans to publish this quarterly data, according to Orrick. A call report is the standard periodic financial filing that banks submit to regulators, so the quarterly form means stablecoin issuers would be reporting in a familiar format.

How many institutions and how much work

The FDIC estimates that about 30 FDIC-supervised insured depository institutions would engage in these activities. It estimates the combined annual burden of weekly and quarterly reporting at 3,840 hours. Dividing, calculated here, gives roughly 128 hours per institution a year, or about two and a half hours a week, though the sources do not say that the burden would be spread evenly, and actual effort would depend on the size of the issuer and the number of stablecoin brands.

What the sources do not say

The sources do not list every data field, do not give reserve composition percentages or redemption figures, and do not describe the Paperwork Reduction Act process in detail. They also do not explain how the FDIC chose the $1 billion and $100 million thresholds. Whether and how the quarterly data would be published alongside the confidentiality of the reports is also not reconciled in the sources.

Why weekly data matters

Reserve backing is the central promise of a payment stablecoin: each token is supposed to be redeemable for a dollar, supported by reserve assets. Weekly reporting by brand lets a supervisor compare issuance with reserves frequently, rather than waiting for a quarterly filing. The forms also ask about large holders and exchanges, which indicate concentration and where redemptions might come from. This reading follows from the schedules the sources describe and is not a statement by the FDIC.

What happens next

After the comment period closes, the FDIC will consider the feedback and decide whether to adopt the forms, possibly with changes. Issuers and banks that expect to issue stablecoins will want to check their systems' ability to produce weekly reserve data by brand. The sources give no effective date. Readers should consult the FDIC's Financial Institution Letter and the Federal Register notice for the exact requirements. This article is general information and not legal advice.
source_name: Orrick (analysis of the FDIC notice, July 24, 2026) and the Independent Community Bankers of America (July 20, 2026)
image_alt: Digital coins and payment technology representing stablecoin regulation (illustrative)
key_points: The FDIC announced a notice on proposed reporting forms and instructions on July 17, 2026 (an ICBA summary is dated July 20), implementing its April 10 proposed rule under the GENIUS Act; comments are due September 18.
Each permitted payment stablecoin issuer (PPSI) would file a separate weekly form for each stablecoin brand it issues, and all PPSIs would file a quarterly report.

The full weekly form, PS-01, applies to issuers with at least $1 billion of outstanding issuance or at least $100 million of average daily transaction volume in the prior month, has eight schedules, and covers reserve assets such as cash, U.S. Treasury securities, reverse repurchase agreements and money market funds.
An abridged form, PS-01a, with three schedules, applies to smaller issuers, and the quarterly form, PS-02, is a streamlined version of bank call reports with five schedules.

The FDIC estimates about 30 FDIC-supervised insured depository institutions would engage in these activities, with a combined annual burden of 3,840 hours, and says the reports would be confidential, though it plans to publish the quarterly data.
why_it_matters: The GENIUS Act created a federal framework for dollar-pegged payment stablecoins. Reporting forms are how supervisors will actually see whether an issuer's reserves match its tokens. This proposal shows the level of detail, down to weekly data per stablecoin brand, that bank-affiliated issuers could be expected to provide.

title: NAB Insurance and CommBank Insurance Join the Resilience Ratings Scheme, Taking Bushfire Premium Discounts to About Half the Australian Home Market
summary: NAB Insurance, underwritten by Allianz, and CommBank Insurance, underwritten by Hollard, have joined NRMA and Suncorp in recognising Resilience Ratings, so households that make bushfire upgrades can earn premium reductions of 5% to 21%, according to the Minister for Home Affairs' announcement and industry coverage.
description:
Two of Australia's biggest bank-branded insurers have joined a scheme that gives households a way to lower their bushfire insurance costs by proving they have made their homes safer. The Minister for Home Affairs announced on July 2, 2026 that NAB Insurance and CommBank Insurance would recognise the Resilience Ratings scheme, and Insurance Business Australia reported that half the home insurance market now prices bushfire mitigation. NAB Insurance is underwritten by Allianz, and CommBank Insurance is underwritten by Hollard. They join NRMA and Suncorp, which already used the ratings.

Resilience Ratings are produced through an app released in October 2023 by the Resilient Building Council. A homeowner answers questions or has an assessor look at the property, and the app produces a star rating that reflects how well the house is protected against bushfire. Typical measures include ember-resistant screens and vents, non-combustible roofing and cladding, and managing vegetation near the home. An insurer that recognises the rating can then use it when setting the premium.

The government's figures set out the potential benefit. Savings can reach A$840 a year for a household, the bushfire component of a premium can be reduced by up to 60 per cent, and total premium reductions range from 5 per cent to 21 per cent. These are ranges and depend on the insurer, the property and the policy, so a household should ask for a quote before assuming a particular discount. The reductions apply to the bushfire element, so a home with a small bushfire component will see a smaller saving than a home in a high-risk fringe area.

Uptake so far is substantial. More than 63,500 households across 324 local government areas have used the app, and more than 19,000 have completed three or more upgrades, spending about A$218 million between them. The Commonwealth provided A$3.2 million of funding. Those figures show that a significant amount of private money has gone into home hardening, which is the point of the scheme: premium relief gives owners a financial reason to pay for changes that also protect their families.

To explain why upgrades matter, NAB cited ratings from the Resilient Building Council. A home rated one or two stars has a 50 to 80 per cent chance of severe damage in a bushfire. For three and four stars, the chance falls to 7 to 18 per cent, and a five-star home has about a 1.5 per cent chance. These are modelled estimates rather than guarantees, but the gap between the lowest and highest ratings is the reason insurers are prepared to differentiate by rating.

The scheme is also expanding to other hazards. A multi-hazard trial now covers 1,000 Queensland households, and the Resilient Building Council estimates that about 1 million homes sit in flood-risk areas, which indicates the possible scale if flood mitigation is built into the same framework. The coverage also referred to the Hazards Insurance Partnership's guiding principles, published in March 2026, which set out how insurers and governments intend to work together on resilience and pricing.

There are limits to what the scheme can do. A rating lowers the price of the risk that a household has reduced, but it does not remove the risk, and it cannot fix problems of affordability that stem from reinsurance costs, building costs and the frequency of disasters. Households in the highest-risk areas may still face high premiums, and some upgrades are expensive. Renters and apartment owners have fewer options, since many of the useful measures concern the structure or the surrounding land.

For homeowners, the sensible next step is to check whether their insurer recognises the rating, ask what discount applies to their postcode and policy, and compare it with the cost of the upgrades. For the industry, the broader significance is that pricing for mitigation is becoming a mainstream feature rather than an experiment. With NAB and CommBank on board, a majority of customers of the largest brands could, in principle, get credit for improving their homes, and the multi-hazard work will show whether the same approach can be applied to floods and storms.

A short example shows how the numbers can be read. If a household's bushfire premium component were a few hundred dollars a year, a 60 per cent cut would be a modest saving, whereas in a high-risk area where the bushfire component is large, the same percentage could amount to hundreds of dollars and approach the stated maximum of A$840. This is an illustration of how percentages work, not a quote, and the announcements do not publish the underlying premium levels. The range of 5 to 21 per cent for total premium reductions suggests that bushfire is only a part of the premium for most households, with other perils such as storm, theft and accidental damage making up the rest.

The assessment process is worth understanding before a household starts spending. Upgrades vary in cost and effect, and the app is designed to show which changes improve the rating most. Households that are considering work should confirm with their insurer which upgrades are recognised and whether a rating needs to be refreshed after changes. Because the scheme is voluntary, a household that does nothing keeps its existing premium basis, and a household that upgrades but is insured with a provider that does not recognise the rating will not receive a discount until it changes insurer or the provider joins.

Looking forward, the participation of NAB and CommBank is a signal to the remaining insurers. If customers can obtain discounts from insurers covering half the market, the competitive pressure on others to accept the ratings or offer equivalent recognition increases. That is a market outcome the announcements describe as momentum rather than as a requirement, and any decision by other insurers remains theirs to make.
source_name: Minister for Home Affairs and Insurance Business Australia (July 2, 2026)
image_alt: Bushfire-prone Australian property representing resilience-based insurance (illustrative)
key_points: NAB Insurance (underwritten by Allianz) and CommBank Insurance (underwritten by Hollard) joined NRMA and Suncorp, so about half of the home insurance market now recognises the scheme.
Savings can reach A$840 a year, the bushfire part of the premium can fall by up to 60%, and total premium reductions range from 5% to 21%.
More than 63,500 households across 324 local government areas have used the app, and over 19,000 have completed three or more upgrades, spending about A$218 million.
The Commonwealth contributed A$3.2 million, and a multi-hazard trial now covers 1,000 Queensland households, with an estimated 1 million homes in flood-risk areas.
NAB-cited ratings put 1 to 2 star homes at a 50% to 80% chance of severe damage in a bushfire, 3 to 4 star homes at 7% to 18% and 5 star homes at about 1.5%.
why_it_matters: Bushfire premiums are among the largest drivers of home insurance affordability problems in high-risk areas. If a property rating is accepted by insurers covering half the market, households have a measurable reason to invest in upgrades, though the discount depends on the policy and the insurer.

title: UK Regulators' Captive Insurance Proposal (CP11/26): Single-Parent Captives, a 4-to-6-Week Authorisation Target and No Solvency UK, With Launch Planned for Summer 2027
summary: The Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority published CP11/26 on July 14, 2026 proposing a tailored regime for single-parent captive insurers, with lower capital and reporting requirements, a joint authorisation process targeting four to six weeks, exclusion from Solvency UK and the Consumer Duty, consultation closing October 14 and launch planned for summer 2027.
description:
Britain wants to be a more attractive home for captive insurers, and its two main financial regulators have now set out how. On July 14, 2026, the Bank of England published a news release announcing that the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority are jointly consulting on a new regime for captive insurance. The consultation paper is PRA CP11/26, titled "A tailored regime for captive insurance". It closed on October 14, 2026, and the regulators say the formal launch is planned for summer 2027, after they have considered the feedback.

A captive is an insurance company that a business owns in order to insure its own risks, instead of buying all its cover from the commercial market. It gives a large organisation more control over pricing, capacity and how it manages its risks. Many multinational groups currently place their captives in other jurisdictions. The proposals are intended to offer a framework that is proportionate to the lower risk that captives pose, since they insure a corporate group's own exposures and not members of the public, while keeping appropriate safeguards.

The first point to understand is the scope. According to the Bank of England release, the proposal covers only single-parent captives, meaning captives that insure or reinsure the risks of their parent and of the parent's group companies. It does not yet cover protected cell companies, structures in which separate cells ring-fence the assets and liabilities of different participants. The regulators say they plan to consult on adding protected cell companies once the legislation needed to do so is in place. Anyone reading the consultation as a general captive regime for every structure should therefore note that this first stage is narrower.

The second point is the lighter prudential treatment. The release says the regulators propose lower capital and reporting requirements for captives, together with a flexible capital resources framework. It gives no capital figures, so the real cost of running a UK captive can only be judged once the detailed rules are published in the consultation paper and finalised. Captives would be excluded from Solvency UK, the prudential regime that applies to the UK's commercial insurers, and from the Consumer Duty, the conduct standard that is aimed at retail customers. The FCA would instead apply tailored conduct requirements, with proportionate supervision and reporting. The PRA would provide dedicated supervisory resource for captives.

The third point is speed. The regulators propose a joint authorisation process with a target of four to six weeks. For a company comparing domiciles, time to authorisation is one of the practical measures of how easy a jurisdiction is to use, and a published target is a commitment the regulators will be judged against. The release does not say what would stop the clock or how the target would be measured, so those details are matters for the consultation paper.

There is one express limit designed to protect employees. Captives may reinsure employee-benefits-related policies but may not insure them directly. The practical effect is that an employee who is covered by a benefits policy would still deal with a conventionally regulated insurer, with the captive standing behind it as reinsurer. This keeps individuals, who are not the intended customers of a captive, outside the lighter regime.

The release carries statements from both regulators. David Bailey, the PRA's executive director for prudential policy, said: "This bespoke regime for captives will enhance the UK's competitive edge in insurance." Sarah Pritchard, the FCA's deputy chief executive, said: "Our approach is pragmatic and proportionate, with appropriate safeguards in place." The release also points to a speech on captives by Shoib Khan at the AIRMIC annual conference on June 16, 2026, which preceded the formal consultation.

The proposals belong to a wider push by UK regulators to give weight to growth and international competitiveness alongside their core duties of protecting policyholders and the stability of the financial system. Supporters of the regime argue that a competitive captive framework would deepen the UK's insurance ecosystem, including the professional services that surround it. The release does not quantify the business expected to move to the UK, and it does not say how many captives might apply, so those arguments are expectations and not forecasts.

The scale of ambition should be kept in proportion. A regime that applies only to single-parent captives, with lighter capital rules, is a targeted offer to a specific kind of customer: corporate groups that want to retain more of their own risk and are weighing where to base the vehicle. It does not change how the UK's commercial insurers are regulated, and the release makes clear that the lighter treatment depends on the captive serving only its own group, which is why the employee-benefits limit and the single-parent restriction matter so much. What happens next is straightforward. The consultation closed on October 14, so the regulators are now reviewing responses. They will publish final rules before the planned launch in summer 2027, and the later work on protected cell companies depends on legislation. Companies thinking about a UK captive should read CP11/26 itself for the proposed capital resources framework, reporting requirements and authorisation steps, and should treat the details described here as proposals, not final rules.
source_name: Bank of England news release (July 14, 2026) on PRA Consultation Paper CP11/26
image_alt: London financial district representing UK insurance regulation (illustrative)
key_points: The PRA and FCA jointly published consultation paper CP11/26, 'A tailored regime for captive insurance', on July 14, 2026; the consultation closed on October 14, 2026 and the regulators say the regime will launch in summer 2027 after feedback is considered.

The proposals cover only single-parent captives, which insure or reinsure the risks of their parent and its group companies; protected cell companies are not yet included, and the regulators plan to consult on them once the necessary legislation is in place.

Lower capital and reporting requirements and a flexible capital resources framework are proposed, though the news release gives no capital figures; captives would be excluded from Solvency UK and from the Consumer Duty.
A joint PRA/FCA authorisation process would target four to six weeks, with dedicated PRA supervisory resource and tailored, proportionate FCA conduct requirements.
As a safeguard for employees, captives could reinsure but not directly insure employee-benefits-related policies.
why_it_matters: Captives are a way for large companies to manage their own risks, and many choose to base them overseas. If the UK regime attracts some of that business, it would bring related work in actuarial, legal and management services onshore, which is the competitiveness argument the regulators and the government are making. For companies deciding where to establish a captive, the practical questions are speed, cost and certainty: a four-to-six-week target and a lighter capital regime address the first two. The proposals are still a consultation, so the final rules, and the capital levels, may change, and the regime will not be open for applications until it launches in 2027.
